text.p: Andre Agassi's comeback trail took another wrong turn Tuesday when rookie Justin Gimelstob beat him 7-5 6-2 Tuesday night in an opening-round match at the $303,000 Infiniti Open.

The setback was the sixth time the former world number one has lost his first match of a tournament this year. The recent funk has the three-time Grand Slam champion wondering when he will return to his winning ways.

"It will take a while to get that confidence back -- to prove to myself I can beat these guys day in and day out again," he added after falling to 6-8 this season. "It's just a grind. You've got to pay the price and do it. I certainly am committed to that challenge and I will do it."

In other matches top seed Goran Igvanisevic of Croatia stopped South African Neville Godwin 7-6 (7-4) 6-3, third seed Mark Philippoussis of Australia blasted 20 aces to overcome Brazil's Roberto Jabali 1-6 6-3 7-6 (7-0) and fourth seed and two-time champion Richard Krajick fired 14 aces to upend Marcos Ondruska of South Africa 6-4 6-4.

Sixth seed Jim Courier of the United States used breaks in the 11th game of each set to dispatch South African Grant Stafford 7-5 7-5 and Sargis Sargsian of Armenia upset eighth-seeded American Alex O'Brien 6-4 6-3.
Agassi admits it is difficult to get back to the top.
"At this stage of the ballgame it makes me feel frustrated and like I cannot do it. So it's a tough hump to get over. It doesn't get any easier week after week," he said.
"As soon as I can get a little progress as far as getting a 'W' the better off I'll be. But I will not allow this to set me back. I refuse to let it get me down."
Agassi returned to play after a 10-week layoff due to a right wrist injury but lost to little-known Doug Flach in Washington, D.C., last week. The result here was the same.
"I still kind of kept getting the lead but not remembering how to win," said Agassi, who has fallen to 32nd in the world after dropping to 6-8 this season.
"That should come along. It's like a woman who's been pregnant 10 months," he said. "All of a sudden it just happens."
The 20-year old Gimelstob, who starred at the University of California at Los Angeles, was elated over his biggest victory ever.

"I had goosebumps when I walked on the court, I was so excited," said Gimelstob, who is ranked 103rd in the world. "I feel the same way now. To have a win like this in front of my friends and family on my home court feels great."
"Obviously, he's not at the top of his game right now but I have so much respect for him," he said. "But I competed well, played a good match and things went my way."
"I'm not going to say he played the match of his life and I beat him. When he plays the match of his life, you're just praying for rain."
Gimelstob captured the opening set, breaking Agassi in the final game for the third time when he cracked a cross-court winner on his fifth break point to end the 17-point game.
Agassi took a brief lead with an immediate break in the second set, but Gimelstob returned the favour twice for a 3-1 advantage.

Gimelstob fought off a break point in the seventh game to go ahead 5-2 before closing out the one-hour, 27-minute match when Agassi committed his fourth and fifth double faults on the final two points of the match.
Agassi was asked if anything postive came out of the defeat.

"It's just another match and we'll take the next step from here," he said. "It didn't set me back as much as I didn't break through. It's not going to take one match to win. It's just another match and next time it will much easier for me to not lose serve after geting up a break."
